question: A 55-year-old man with a history of repeated hospitalization for chronic pancreatitis comes to the physician because of difficulty walking and standing steadily. Neurological examination shows an unsteady, broad-based gait, distal muscle weakness, decreased deep tendon reflexes, and an abnormal Romberg test. His hemoglobin concentration is 11.9 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 89/μm3, and serum lactate dehydrogenase is 105 U/L. His serum haptoglobin is slightly decreased. A deficiency of which of the following substances is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Chronic pancreatitis" -> "Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins" -> "Possible deficiency in tocopherol (Vitamin E)" -> 70% CHAIN: "Chronic pancreatitis" -> "Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins" -> "Possible deficiency in phytomenadione (Vitamin K)" -> 60% CHAIN: "Chronic pancreatitis" -> "Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins" -> "Possible deficiency in pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)" -> 50% CHAIN: "Chronic pancreatitis" -> "Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins" -> "Possible deficiency in niacin (Vitamin B3)" -> 40% CHAIN: "Chronic pancreatitis" -> "Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins" -> "Possible deficiency in folate (Vitamin B9)" -> 70%
analysis: The patient's presentation with neurological symptoms, including unsteady gait, muscle weakness, decreased deep tendon reflexes, and abnormal Romberg test, along with laboratory findings of decreased haptoglobin and macrocytic anemia, is suggestive of a peripheral neuropathy. Given the history of chronic pancreatitis, the most likely cause of these findings is a deficiency in vitamin E (Tocopherol), which can lead to neurological manifestations.
